lignes.texte: Those gruelling workouts aren’t building your physique. They’re eating it alive.
If you push a broken, burnt out body to the limit,
your system goes straight into panic mode. It sees all that fresh damage and does whatever
it takes to survive… by stripping fuel straight off your chest, back and arms.
You leave the gym thinking you got bigger… your body just cannibalized what was already there..
These are the 10 reasons you’re wrecking your physique…
When people start working out, they try to do two opposite things at once:
slash their calories and crush themselves in the gym. On paper, it makes sense.
Eat less, burn more, get lean.
But in reality, you just backed your metabolism into a corner.
Your body doesn’t care about your aesthetic goals. All it cares about is survival. And despite what
the gym bros say, your body doesn’t burn pure body fat while leaving lean muscle alone.
Whenever you drop weight, it’s estimated around 25% of that loss will be from muscle.
This is the nightmare scenario with GLP-1 medications like Ozempic or Wegovy.
Because the fat drops off at breakneck speeds, patients frequently lose large amounts of
lean mass alongside it. Doctors usually have to step in and protect the user’s skeletal muscle.
And millions of natural lifters are experiencing this same biological disaster on their own.
Because the body has specific appetites.
The moment you cut your calories, your body raids its emergency reserves.
It burns through your stored glycogen in a matter of hours. Once that tank is empty,
it starts burning fat and converting muscle protein to glucose. Which means that if you’re
not maintaining your body’s equilibrium, it’ll wind up turning against declaring war against you.
If you’re just looking to get healthy, it’s nothing to worry about. But if
you’re specifically looking to get jacked, your own body is devouring your hard work.
And the sabotage begins the moment you sit down to eat…
One of the biggest mistakes people make when trying to build muscle
is assuming that they need to eat clean. Lifters usually swing between two extremes:
they either jump on a strict post-holiday diet,
or they buy into a special diet that is often advertised by shady podcasters or influencers.
But there isn’t some sort of special hack that works to build muscle. It’s all about feeding
your body properly to ensure it has the energy and storage it needs for some pretty heavy workouts.
And none of the hyped diets are correct.
Most diets advertise shortcuts to health by depriving your body of something.
But working out is putting your body through stress. So when it comes to protein,
it’s non-negotiable. The average guideline for protein intake is around 0.61 to 0.73 grams per
pound (1.35 to 1.6 grams per kilogram) of body weight. A typical serving size is around 20 grams.
But many people make the mistake of sticking to single incomplete proteins
or try to make do with isolated vegan options that lack the amino acids to stimulate muscle growth.
And the damage gets worse if you starve your body.
Most of the fad diets encourage people to eschew carbohydrates, because that helps the body lose
weight fast. But the opposite is true for building muscle. The body needs carbs for energy, and if it
can’t find them in the stomach, it’ll find them in the muscle tissue and start breaking it down.
There’s a reason that marathon runners typically have a huge pasta meal before race day.
But for ideal health, whole grains, fruits, and vegetables are the ideal partner for your protein.
It’s also important to make sure that you’re getting the right vitamins.
Studies show that over 30% of gym-goers and athletes suffer from micronutrient deficiencies,
which affect their body chemistry. Lacking Vitamin A, Vitamin D, Zinc, or Magnesium
can mean your body isn’t processing fuel and effort in the most efficient way.
Now that you’re fueled, it’s time to get working.
If you talk to a lot of other gym-goers, you’ll probably get the same advice:
you want to feel the burn!
That advice is ingrained in a lot of people, and it leads them to push their limits constantly.
They work out until they’re ready to collapse, head home,
take an aspirin to dull the aches, and return to the gym the next day.
But that might actually be slowing down your progress.
Surprisingly, working out isn’t where your muscles actually grow. They’re being strained
and pulled to their limits during workouts, and this causes invisible, microscopic damage that
your body slowly heals. And that healing happens while you’re resting, as your body can slowly
recover and come back stronger. But many people don’t give their body that chance to recover,
instead trying to smash the gym every day. They trap their body in a neverending loop of the
dreaded DOMS, or Delayed Onset Muscle Soreness. Their strength doesn’t increase, it declines.
So ironically, the way to do more… is to do less.
Experts recommend against going to the gym every day, especially if you’re just starting out.
Instead, take 1 to 2 rest days between each workout, listen to your body, and only go
back when any pain has subsided. One of the most important things you can do to build muscle is to
view recovery as just as important as the active workout. Light exercise to stay active is fine,
but on the days you’re not working out, your body is… and it prefers to work silently and in peace.
And you’ve got to make sure everyone gets a turn.
Every fitness feed is drowning in the same manta: “Feel the Burn! Embrace the Grind!”.
It creates a picture where everyone assumes that the harder you’re working,
the better you’re doing. As long as you leave the gym covered in sweat and gasping for air,
you’re doing something right.
But in reality, the body isn’t a steam crank that just needs to get rolling. It’s a finely
calibrated machine that needs to be maintained. If you redline it, it’ll probably tear itself apart.
It’s a mistake that can happen in the first session.
Many people dive straight into intense cardio to give them the feeling of working hard.
Power walking evolves into jogging.
Or they obliterate themselves with High-Intensity Interval Training.
These sessions get the heart pumping and your lungs screaming.
So it feels productive, but it doesn’t build muscle.
For that, you need to lift.
Each individual muscle group needs to be treated like its own machine.
You can’t expect to grow your arms and legs from running. And you can’t expect your chest,
back and shoulders to get defined without targeted resistance. It’s important to work your
way through each part of the body to grow muscle naturally and keep the body in the ideal shape.
But there can easily be too much of a good thing.
When lifting weights, people make two common mistakes. One is sticking with the same weight
for an extended period and then not doing anything to push that little bit further.
Eventually, the body will get used to this workout and it’ll stop being as effective.
This makes it little more than light exercise, and you won’t build any significant amount of muscle.
But the other, more serious mistake is trying to go too fast. If you haven’t
been working out for a while, it’s easy to overestimate your ability.
And we’ve all seen it happen at the gym.
But even with smaller weights, it’s easy to strain or even tear muscles,
which can set back workouts for weeks or months. But not all damage is visible to the naked eye.
We come back to “the burn”, which is the sign of your body working hard.
But when you feel it, the body needs to get that energy back.
One of the biggest ironies of trying to build muscle is that our own bodies are quick to absorb
it right back. The body views muscle as expensive luxury tissue when it’s under high stress,
and many people put the body under that stress by working out just a little too hard.
Your body is your best guide through the workout process, and if it’s complaining too much, it’s
probably time to dial it back. Besides, if you’re rotating your workouts properly, strength training
and weights will get enough of a break between sessions that your body will have time to rebound.
But too little of a good thing can be a problem too.
Unfortunately, today people are bombarded constantly with advice
on the best way to get fit. Some of this advice can come from trusted sources,
like a doctor or trainer. But other pieces of advice come from the guys at the gym,
trying to be helpful. And that’s before you get to the barrage of information from the internet,
clickbaiting you with that perfect workout regimen for rock-hard abs.
And too many people listen to it.
A good workout routine is varied, but it’s not random.
The goal of consistent workouts is progressive overload,
which is when your body is pushed to its limit, has the chance to recover,
and is then pushed just a little bit further. Each session extends your endurance just a bit,
and the body is able to gain muscle, recover, and then gain more. But people start a routine,
then switch it up because they heard different advice. Suddenly, a whole new muscle group is
being worked out, and the body doesn’t know where to concentrate its efforts.
And that means a lot of your effort might be going down the drain.
The problem with a workout routine that incorporates too many things, without a set
schedule that builds on past gains, is that all your effort is going into different activities.
This kind of scattered workout can be effective if you’re looking to build general endurance,
lose some weight, and improve your health. But the gains will almost all be invisible.
You won’t see consistent muscle gain unless you’re sticking to
a routine that gives your muscle groups the chance to build themselves up consistently.
But if you push yourself too far, your body will let you know.
It can be easy to focus on your strong points, but the truth is that it’s not always your lack
of strength or willpower holding you back. Your weakest points are more likely to let you down.
If you feel standard, warm soreness after a workout, your body is responding to
exceptional effort. So, it’s probably best to listen and give it time to recover.
But if you feel a sudden pain while working out, especially in a joint,
it’s potentially the sign of a much bigger issue… one that could come back to haunt you.
This is how many gains are lost.
Nothing knocks a muscle gain program off track faster than an injury.
Not only does it make it impossible to work that area out until it heals,
but a knee or ankle injury can essentially knock an athlete out of commission for weeks. Muscles
can atrophy and return to their pre-workout levels or worse. The best approach when dealing with a
painful area is to visit with a doctor or trainer. It’s often as simple as getting a light support
brace to use while working out, to add a little extra support when pushing it to your limits.
But your body might not even be responding like you hope.
Even if you’re not injuring yourself, it may not be beneficial to push your body too far. Your
muscles receive most of the signals that it’s time to repair and grow through the first few workout
sets. Once those are past, the added workout is classified as “junk volume” - exercise that
increases fatigue and risk of injury, but without adding any real benefit. Experts recommend that
after a few hard sets, it’s best to step away and switch to working out a different muscle group.
But for many people, they stop just when they’re about to hit the sweet spot.
We’ve all been there. We take a week off, say we’ll be back,
and then next thing we know we’re right back where we started. For some,
it just becomes a running gag, but for others, it’s a more serious question.
Exactly how much of a break can you take before you start losing the hard work you put into it?
The good news is, there’s a bit more leeway than you might have thought.
While we’d all like to be consistently doing 3 to 5 sessions a week, real life tends to get in
the way. Getting to the gym can be a little too challenging some days, and it’s easy to worry
about when muscle loss can creep in. But a recent study shows that maintaining gains can be easier
than thought. Two sample groups completed a consistent, 12-week period of resistance
and aerobic training, and were then released to follow a pair of different maintenance routines.
One group did a training session every 7 days, while the other only returned to the
gym once every 2 weeks. A third group, meanwhile, stopped training altogether.
And the results were promising for those in a time crunch.
The third group experienced a fairly significant loss of muscle strength and aerobic fitness,
while the 14-day group also saw significant reduction. However, the 7-day group saw only
minor reductions across the board, with most of their gains being maintained.
This indicates that while working out once a week probably won’t be enough to consistently
build muscle, it’s enough to maintain gains. So for many people, building muscle might be
a longer process that ramps up only when they have time for it, and that’s fine.
But surprisingly, one of the most important things you can do for building muscle
happens when you’re not working out at all.
If you’re having trouble getting to the gym because of lack of time, the odds
are you’re not sleeping enough either. Over 30% of people in the United States
report getting less than 7 hours of sleep a night. This is even more profound in teenagers,
where 77% of teens don’t hit the recommended amount of sleep. But after a while,
most people report getting used to it. They’re always a little tired,
but they’re able to function from day to day in their life with that undercurrent of fatigue.
But that doesn’t mean the body doesn’t remember.
Lack of sleep is one of the most common culprits for the body not being able to gain muscle mass,
and it’s also one of the hardest to detect. While lack of sleep might only cause invisible damage,
it unbalances just about every major system in the body and affects the healing process.
As building muscle relies on that process, you’re directly undercutting
your gains by not getting enough sleep. The process of muscle protein synthesis,
which the body uses to build and repair tissue, is reduced by around 18% if you’re not getting
enough sleep. Sleep deprivation also spikes cortisol, the hormone that breaks down muscle,
by over 21%. Testosterone, which is essential for maintaining energy, drops by 24%.
You’re sabotaging your own progress without even knowing it.
Your body is a biological construction crew, and deliberately leaving it short-staffed is
setting yourself up to fail. That means, for many, the most important thing they can do to
maintain their progress is to ironically do less. Setting the alarm for a half-hour later may mean
more to long-term muscle gain than getting in another set of the same exercises at the gym.
But all of these issues come together into one final mistake
that may be sabotaging all your hard work.
The biggest mistake many people make when working out is… not doing their homework.
You can work out at the gym and try to eat right,
but it doesn’t take much to undermine all that hard work. If you’re not keeping track
of exactly what you’re doing and when you’re doing it, you’re flying blind.
And you’re more likely to crash.
So your first stop on a workout journey might be the app store?
A tracking app can be a life-changer when it comes to a workout routine. Every time you work out,
you can input the day you went to the gym and the type of workout you did. It makes it easy to avoid
overworking specific muscle groups and to ensure you’re getting in at least one workout a week.
If your app has the capability, you can also track calorie and nutrient intake and sleep
time each night, to create a full picture of how you’re maintaining your current routine.
With a busy life, the brain cannot keep track of everything alone.
You’re fueling a powerful machine. Give it the support it needs.
The process of building a better body is long and intense, and many people are trying to do
it without the support they need from themselves. It’s like trying to build
a skyscraper while the ground crew is actively digging up the foundation. But the good news is,
it’s not that you need to work harder. In most cases, it’s that you need to work smarter,
making sure that each workout counts because you’re giving your body the backup it needs.
So, you’ve been exercising, eating better, and doing everything right,
but you still have that little chubby spot. Why? Watch “Why You Can’t Lose Fat in THIS
Area (And Other Weight Loss Facts)“ to find out why it won’t budge. Or click on this.
